content.title: About
content.content: The “American and Swiss” cheese blend combines processed American cheese with Swiss cheese featuring characteristic holes. It has a smooth, slightly creamy texture, a moderately sharp flavor, and a pleasant aroma, suitable for both hot and cold dishes.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: American cheese was created in the early 20th century in the USA as a cost‑effective cheese alternative.
Swiss cheese (Emmental) is known for its “eyes,” formed by carbon dioxide released by bacteria.
The blend merges the meltability of American cheese with the aromatic notes of Swiss, making it popular in fast‑food applications.
It is commonly used in sandwiches, burgers, casseroles, and fondue.
Combining the two cheeses improves stretchability and gives a richer taste than either cheese alone.

items.title: Calcium source
items.content: Cheese is rich in calcium, essential for strong bones and teeth.

items.title: Protein
items.content: Provides high‑quality dairy protein that supports tissue growth and repair.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Contains vitamins B2 and B12, which aid energy metabolism.

items.title: Phosphorus
items.content: Phosphorus contributes to cellular function and nervous system health.

items.title: Probiotic cultures
items.content: Swiss cheese includes live bacteria that can benefit gut health.

items.title: Lactose intolerance
items.content: The blend contains lactose, so individuals with intolerance should limit intake.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: It can be salty; excess sodium may increase blood pressure risk.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: Some people may experience allergic reactions to casein.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Cheese is high in fat and calories, so portion control is advised.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Use the blend in hot sandwiches, burgers, casseroles, pasta dishes, or as a cold topping for salads and appetizers. It can be sliced thinly or melted into sauces.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the cheese in the refrigerator at 2‑4 °C in its original packaging or an airtight container. For longer storage, it can be frozen, though texture may change.

egg-white-omelet-scrambled-or-fried-with.title: Egg white, omelet, scrambled, or fried, with meat and vegetables

content.title: About
content.content: The dish consists of egg white prepared as an omelet, scrambled eggs, or fried, combined with lean meat (such as chicken, turkey, or lean beef) and a variety of vegetables (tomatoes, spinach, bell pepper, onion). It provides high‑quality protein, vitamins and minerals, while being low in fat and carbohydrates.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Egg white is almost pure protein and contains virtually no fat or carbs.
Cooking egg white without the yolk reduces the cholesterol content of the meal.
Pairing protein with vegetables increases the bioavailability of certain nutrients, e.g., vitamin C from tomatoes enhances iron absorption from meat.
Quick cooking methods (scrambling or frying) preserve heat‑sensitive vitamins such as vitamin B6.
The dish can be prepared in a microwave or skillet in 5‑10 minutes, making it popular among people with busy lifestyles.

items.title: High protein content
items.content: Egg white and meat supply a complete set of essential amino acids, supporting muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Low fat
items.content: Absence of yolk and use of lean meat keep the dish suitable for low‑fat diets.

items.title: Rich in B‑vitamins
items.content: The meal provides riboflavin (B2), pyridoxine (B6) and cobalamin (B12), important for energy metabolism and nervous system health.

items.title: Source of minerals
items.content: Meat and vegetables deliver iron, zinc, magnesium and potassium, supporting electrolyte balance.

items.title: Immune support
items.content: Vitamin C from vegetables and antioxidant properties of egg white help strengthen immune defenses.

items.title: Egg allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to egg white, ranging from skin rashes to anaphylaxis.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Using processed meat or sauces can raise sodium levels; opt for fresh, unsalted meat and season lightly.

items.title: Over‑cooking
items.content: Excessive browning can produce acrylamide, a potentially harmful compound.

items.title: Portion control
items.content: Large servings may lead to excess calories, especially if the dish is prepared with added oil.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Whisk the egg white, add diced lean meat and chopped vegetables. In a lightly oiled hot skillet, cook as an omelet, scramble, or fry, stirring until the egg white is fully set. Season with salt, pepper and herbs as desired.

content.title: Storage
content.content: The prepared dish is best eaten fresh. If needed, store in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 24 hours. Reheat in a skillet or microwave to retain texture.

content.title: About
content.content: Scalloped potato made from fresh tubers is a classic dish where thinly sliced potatoes are baked in a creamy sauce of milk, butter, cheese and seasonings until a golden crust forms.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The dish is popular in North American and European cuisines as a side or a main course.
Thin slices allow the potatoes to absorb the sauce quickly and cook evenly.
The cream sauce is often flavored with nutmeg, which enhances the potato flavor.
Baking creates a crisp top while keeping the interior tender.
Traditionally served hot, garnished with fresh herbs.

items.title: Rich in potassium
items.content: Potatoes provide potassium, which supports normal blood pressure and muscle function.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Contains vitamin B6 and niacin, important for metabolism and nervous system health.

items.title: Energy source
items.content: Carbohydrates give a quick source of energy, useful after physical activity.

items.title: Dietary fiber
items.content: Provides fiber that aids healthy digestion.

items.title: Calcium from cream
items.content: The creamy sauce adds calcium, essential for bones and teeth.

items.title: High calorie content
items.content: The cream sauce and cheese make the dish calorie‑dense; portion control is recommended.

items.title: Lactose presence
items.content: People with lactose intolerance may experience discomfort from the dairy ingredients.

items.title: Sodium level
items.content: Added salt and cheese increase sodium, which can be a concern for hypertension.

items.title: Dairy allergy
items.content: Allergy to milk or cheese requires substitution with plant‑based alternatives.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve hot as a side to meat, fish or poultry, or enjoy it as a main dish. Top with fresh herbs, fried onions or additional seasonings to taste.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Leftover scalloped potatoes keep in the refrigerator for up to 3 days in an airtight container. Reheat in the oven to restore the crispy crust.
